guest.bio_context: Dr. V spent nearly a decade at Lightspeed Venture Partners before spinning out to start a new fund. context.transcript_excerpt: Dr. V, you spent nearly a decade at Lightspeed before deciding to spin out. And before we started recording, you said that the market right now is undervalued. Why is that? This is something I learned from Chris Shepi, who was one of the founders of Lightspeed. He said the market always seems to be overvaluing technology. And 10 years later, you realize it wasn't. I've kind of like learned to tune these things out. But you look at the data, right? I mean, if you look at, let's say, 2000 and 2009, when I was starting my first company on the aftermath of global financial crisis. The total market cap of private technology companies at that time was maybe close to $15 to $80 billion. And then the largest company was Facebook, $15 to $20 billion in market cap. And you fast forward today, we're talking about multi-trillion dollar companies. We're talking about a private market that's in aggregate of about $5 trillion. If somebody had said we would be sitting at a $5 trillion of private market cap even three years or four years ago, it might have seemed ludicrous, right? And here we are. And mind you, we've only seen AI disrupt coding in the world in a realistic way. Most of the revenue of Anthropic and OpenAI are coming from coding. So whether it's medicine, engineering, physical automation, when I look at the degrees of possibility, it just feels very, very large. And the very rough back of the envelope math on that is market cap of the private companies versus venture capital going after those private companies. For perspective, if back in 2008, 2009, the top funds in Silicon Valley were probably raising like $500 to $1 billion funds. And even that was like, wow, that's crazy. There was no SoftBank $100 billion vision fund. There are no mega hedge funds. And I look at like even just Lightspeed, Andreessen, Sequoia, now increasingly, interestingly, Benchmark and any others, like you're already in excess of $50 to $70 billion. The markets have completely reset in terms of the capital scale and expected value. And the big unknown is whether AI will actually disrupt labor. I don't think it's an unknown, right? If you look at the impact that Cursor and Claw are having on coding, which is inherently engineering labor, from like writing sophisticated code and research level code to implementing basic systems, like systems implementation and stuff, very different levels of sophistication. And you're seeing AI kind of eat into a whole bunch of that. For me, the question is less whether it can disrupt labor. The question is what kinds of labor get disrupted first. My point of view is that categories of labor where there is low cost to going wrong, i.e. there's a little bit of course correct available. You don't require a lot of trust. And then second, ones where there's a deterministic right answer and you can actually close the feedback loop, improve the model on a continual basis, which is why coding is so perfect, right? Because when a code is written, it's expected to perform in a certain way. It either works or it does not. Along those two axes, you're going to see things evolve. And if one end is coding, probably the other extreme end is medicine. Cost of going wrong is very high because of multi-systemic nature of biology. pending_qa.q: How has the venture capital playbook fundamentally changed over the past decade?
pending_qa.r: Ten years ago, venture was a reputation business where investors built decades-long track records. Today, sourcing especially at early stage is a media business, with distribution becoming critical for venture firms to see the best opportunities. At exit, investors now proactively manage liquidity through continuation funds, GP secondaries, LP secondaries, and M&A relationships, rather than relying on the old model where one or two investments would go public.

pending_qa.q: What is the primary function of a venture capital firm's capital markets team?
pending_qa.r: The capital markets team segments a venture fund's portfolio of companies into buy, hold, or sell categories. For a large firm with 30-50 investors and thousands of companies, achieving this clarity requires significant work. The team also develops ecosystem relationships to enable exits through tools like continuation funds, GP secondaries, LP secondaries, and M&A partnerships.

pending_qa.q: Which new participant categories are expanding their presence in private markets?
pending_qa.r: Family offices are becoming more switched on to alternative assets and making direct investments in companies. Sovereign wealth funds, which manage approximately $15 trillion in capital, are now significant participants in private markets despite historically not investing in alternatives. About a third of sovereign wealth is being invested in private markets, with roughly two-thirds of that going to direct investments in company stakes rather than through private equity funds.

pending_qa.q: What structural challenges prevent institutional LPs from participating in co-investment opportunities?
pending_qa.r: Most institutional LPs are not equipped for rapid decision-making. Co-investment opportunities often require decisions within less than five days with meaningful capital amounts, but typical LPs only meet once or twice a month in investment committees, making it impossible to act. While 99% of LPs say they want to co-invest, probably only 2-10% actually do on a regular basis.

pending_qa.q: How do multi-stage venture firms expand beyond their core competency, and what is the historical precedent?
pending_qa.r: Private equity firms like KKR and Blackstone emerged with one core business and over time expanded into adjacent asset management. Blackstone started as a real estate private equity investor in early days, but real estate is now their biggest business. Similarly, venture firms that became famous for venture capital are increasingly expanding into buyouts, multi-stage strategies, and adjacent asset classes, though different firms take different risk approaches.

pending_qa.q: What common cognitive bias limits venture investors' deal sourcing and reduces returns?
pending_qa.r: Venture investors have historically relied on their networks to surface opportunities, creating a bias where they miss high-quality outsiders. Founders of Airbnb, Stripe, and many other iconic companies began as total outsiders without network connections. Additionally, markups have become a primary performance metric for young investors within large firms, incentivizing them to chase hot trends rather than contrarian bets one standard deviation away, which ultimately leads to competitive returns on those hot opportunities.
